A few ideas about practical discussions- setting aside enjoyment as a separate subject.

Whose money is whose, and how are expenses going to be divided? What about vacations? I guess everyone could buy their own car, but there are bound to be things coming up that will need to be either shared or not. Someone could get very sick, or be in an accident. How will you handle it together? At least some general idea of what can be expected...

If you're actually thinking about a long term relationship, assume your SO will find someone also, and can not be kept from making the same arrangement with whoever he/she finds. And the current paramour will have to accept several things, i.e. that their desires may not be fully considered in such a case, since they come late to the deal. Kids: does it become a global village, or are you and SO going to hold the full reins and discipline if Paramour is mistreated, or feels they are? Lots of divisiveness available here at the drop of a hat.

Boils down to an echo of the marriage promises: to have and to hold, for better or worse, in sickness and in health, and so on. You want to be sure you understand what the rough is really going to be before you dive into the smooth.

Just learned about Plex and I am trying to find out if it is a good way to setup a home media server. I don't understand what parts are free versus paid and whether you need that extra functionality. For example, I saw the ability to sync with dropbox as part of the paid subscription but why would I pay Plex for using Dropbox? Is it just to access that ability to sync with Dropbox?
What alternatives to Plex have you used and why (or why not) would you go with Plex over these others?

Plex has a few perplexing "premium" options, but it's not really a back stabbing type of premium lock down. I noticed that while the server software is free, the client software often is a trial, and you don't find this out til one day it decides to let you know you're locked out from using THAT client app (for instance, the Roku "channel").

Using the Plex server with a DLNA type client generally works well, but you cannot always play/pause/etc, and it won't support subtitles. I've been looking for a Plex alternative, and as far as ease of use and guarantee that it will work as advertised - Plex is unbeatable.

Before PLex, I used Twonky, which was far better imo - never a hickup, it played everything I threw at it and was the most compatible with media types server side and it was rare that I would find a client that couldn't stream from it. For some retarded reason they changed it up and shutdown the bits I liked.

How are you using Plex? If you're just using it to stream form your PC to some type of set top box, then I would suggest a Chromecast - for 30-35 bucks, you can use Plex+Chrome to stream local media to the Chromecast, and if you use YouTube, Netflix, Hulu, or other supported services, the Chromecast will stream the content directly from the given service, bypassing the internet>PC>router>Chromecast chain.

So if you're trying to stream local media (files that are physically on your PC), Plex is the best that I have seen currently. It has the best compatibility with files and clients. From what I've seen, if all you want to do is stream local media to a non-Plex client, then the free stuff will cover you.

Basically, you either pay for a plex pass, and get everything (including some premium features and platform apps) included, or you pay for the apps individually. When it was $75, it was kind of a no-brainer, especially because I travel internationally and the data speeds tend to be too low for streaming (but I can leave my device near the AP all night and pull down updated media.) But at $150, it's a bit harder to justify.

It depends on what you are doing. Plex is good at being able to stream to literally anywhere. If I was starting from scratch. I'd probably try Emby. It seems to be a competitor, but since I've got a lifetime PlexPass (got it when it was $75), I can't be bothered to try it.
